sections.text: Three Phase 2 trials of IL-17A inhibition in multiple sclerosis have been conducted, all by Novartis using secukinumab (AIN457).

One of the three trials was terminated early due to strategic development priorities, not safety concerns, with Novartis shifting to another anti-IL-17 antibody deemed to have better potential for MS.
Secukinumab has reached Phase 4 for psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis, but not for multiple sclerosis.
Ixekizumab, another IL-17A inhibitor, has also reached Phase 4 for psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis but has not advanced in multiple sclerosis.
The FDA label for secukinumab includes no indication for multiple sclerosis and notes an increased risk of infections and candidiasis, with caution advised for inflammatory bowel disease.

A 2026 study in HLA-DR3 transgenic mice with EAE found that IL-17A is dispensable for brain-predominant disease in the absence of IFNγ, suggesting it may not be essential for all forms of neuroinflammation in MS models.

Recent literature indicates Th17 cells and IL-17A are involved in MS pathogenesis, but their necessity is unclear, with studies showing disease can develop in their absence depending on immune context.

read: Mechanism evidence: IL-17A inhibition has been tested in three Phase 2 trials for MS with no advancement, and recent studies suggest it may not be essential in all neuroinflammatory contexts.
Competitive position: IL-17A inhibitors are approved for other autoimmune conditions but have not progressed in MS; development was deprioritized despite no major safety signals.
Open questions: Is IL-17A necessary for MS pathogenesis given evidence of disease in its absence? Could other Th17-related pathways be more critical?
would_change: New evidence of clinical efficacy in a Phase 2 or Phase 3 trial would change this judgement.
Stronger mechanistic evidence linking IL-17A directly to MS pathology in human-relevant models would support reconsideration.
